items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A theory that the same characteristics make a leader effective in all situations”.
items.answer: Universalist theory of leadership
items.markingKey: Universalist theory of leadership: a theory that the same characteristics make a leader effective in all situations. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Behavioural theories of leadership suggest that leadership can be trained. Reason (R): Behaviours such as consideration can be learned. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: If leadership is behaviour, it can be taught. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Universalist theories of leadership take the situation into account. Reason (R): Universalist theories propose qualities that are effective in all situations. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: They ignore the situation, so the assertion is false. [1]

items.stem: Felix, a new manager at a bank in Muscat, focuses entirely on targets and deadlines and rarely talks to staff about their concerns. Staff turnover has risen. Suggest how Felix could become a 9,9 leader.
items.answer: Keep clear goals while involving staff in decisions, listening to concerns and showing appreciation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark people; 1 mark production [2]

items.stem: Daniel, a new manager at a bank in Kathmandu, focuses entirely on targets and deadlines and rarely talks to staff about their concerns. Staff turnover has risen. (a) Identify Daniel’s position on Blake and Mouton’s managerial grid. (b) Using the Ohio State dimensions, explain why turnover may have risen.
items.answer: (a) Authority-compliance (9,1): high concern for production, low concern for people. (b) High initiating structure with low consideration leaves staff feeling unvalued, reducing satisfaction and increasing turnover.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark low consideration; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the Ohio State behavioural studies of leadership. Include at least one point about self-report.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Identifying behaviours means leaders can be trained in consideration and structure. Strength (measurement): The LBDQ gives quantitative ratings of leader behaviour from followers. Weakness (self-report): Followers’ ratings of leaders may be biased by how much they like the leader. Weakness (situational factors): The best combination of behaviours depends on the situation, which the approach does not fully explain. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The universalist idea that leaders are born with traits that make them great”?
items.answer: Great man theory
items.markingKey: Great man theory: the universalist idea that leaders are born with traits that make them great. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Transformational leaders mainly motivate followers through rewards and punishments.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. That is transactional leadership; transformational leaders inspire with vision and charisma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between universalist and behavioural theories of leadership.
items.answer: Universalist theories focus on who the leader is (traits, charisma) and assume these work everywhere; behavioural theories focus on what the leader does (for example consideration and initiating structure), which can be observed and learned.
items.markingKey: 1 mark universalist; 1 mark behavioural; 1 mark difference made explicit [3]

items.stem: A retail chain in Mumbai compared customer-satisfaction ratings (out of 100) for 7 stores whose managers had completed training in considerate leadership and 7 stores whose managers had not. Table: Satisfaction score (out of 100) — Trained: 68, 83, 74, 78, 71, 67, 69. Untrained: 72, 80, 59, 66, 67, 66, 74. Calculate the median score for the trained condition.
items.markingKey: Ordered scores: 67, 68, 69, 71, 74, 78, 83; median = 71. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2]

items.answer: (a) High initiating structure with low consideration leaves staff feeling unvalued, reducing satisfaction and increasing turnover. (b) Keep clear goals while involving staff in decisions, listening to concerns and showing appreciation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark low consideration; 1 mark effect [2] (b) 1 mark people; 1 mark production [2]

items.stem: Zara has just become supervisor of a new team of inexperienced call-centre staff in Muscat. The procedures are unclear and staff are anxious. Using path-goal theory, suggest which leader behaviour Zara should use and explain why.

items.stem: “Fiedler’s contingency theory of leadership has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including measurement validity in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Organisations can match leaders to situations or change the situation (for example task structure). Strength (situational factors): It recognises that no single style is best, so it explains why leaders succeed in one role but fail in another. Weakness (measurement validity): It is unclear what the LPC scale really measures, and scores may change over time. Weakness (flexibility): It assumes style is fixed, ignoring evidence that leaders can adapt their behaviour. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: A student writes: “In Fiedler’s model, a leader with good relations, a structured task and strong position power is in a very favourable situation.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. All three factors favour the leader.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how Fiedler measured leadership style.
items.answer: Leaders rated their least preferred co-worker on 18 bipolar adjective scales (such as unfriendly–friendly) from 1 to 8; a high total shows the leader can still see the co-worker positively (relationship-motivated), a low total shows task motivation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark LPC rating; 1 mark scoring; 1 mark interpretation [3]

Fiedler classified totals of 73 or more as high LPC and 54 or less as low LPC. Sofia’s team has poor leader–member relations, an unstructured task and weak position power. What is the manager’s total LPC score?

Leila, a manager in Jakarta, completed Fiedler’s LPC scale. The 18 item ratings (1–8) were: 1, 7, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 5, 1, 4, 5, 5, 6, 3, 8, 3, 2, 2. items.answer: (a) 59 (b) In the middle range (neither clearly high nor clearly low LPC)

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the relationship between leaders and followers is the most important factor in leadership. In your answer, you may refer to individual differences and ethics.
items.answer: Arguments for: LMX theory shows that high-quality exchanges lead to better performance, satisfaction and lower turnover. Leader–member relations are the most important factor in Fiedler’s situational favourableness. Arguments against: Leader behaviour (initiating structure) and the task also matter. In-groups and out-groups can create unfairness in teams. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The theory that leaders form relationships of different quality with each follower, creating in-groups and out-groups”?
items.answer: Leader–member exchange (LMX) theory
items.markingKey: Leader–member exchange (LMX) theory: the theory that leaders form relationships of different quality with each follower, creating in-groups and out-groups. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): LMX theory differs from many leadership theories. Reason (R): It focuses on the relationship between the leader and each individual follower. Choose the correct option.

A is true, but R is false.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by in-groups and out-groups in LMX theory.
items.answer: In-group members have high-quality relationships with trust, support and extra responsibilities beyond the contract; out-group members have low-quality relationships limited to formal job requirements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark in-group; 1 mark out-group [2]

items.stem: In an engineering team in Jakarta, Mohammed is often given interesting projects and chats with the manager daily, while Chloe receives only routine tasks and formal instructions. Explain how this difference may affect Chloe’s job satisfaction.
items.answer: Chloe receives less support, trust and opportunity, so is likely to be less satisfied and more likely to leave.
items.markingKey: 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: In an engineering team in Kathmandu, Jonas is often given interesting projects and chats with the manager daily, while Lina receives only routine tasks and formal instructions. (a) Using LMX theory, identify which group each employee belongs to. (b) Explain how this difference may affect Lina’s job satisfaction.
items.answer: (a) Jonas is in the in-group; Lina is in the out-group. (b) Lina receives less support, trust and opportunity, so is likely to be less satisfied and more likely to leave.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: “Leader–member exchange (LMX) theory has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including cause and effect in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (research support): High-quality LMX has been linked to better performance, satisfaction and lower turnover. Strength (usefulness): It explains why some employees are more satisfied and committed than others under the same leader. Weakness (cause and effect): Most evidence is correlational, so good performance may cause a good relationship rather than the reverse. Weakness (ethics): It may seem to justify favouritism and unequal treatment of out-group members. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. items.stem: Explain one ethical problem with LMX theory.
items.answer: Leaders favouring an in-group may treat out-group members unfairly, for example giving them fewer opportunities, which can be discriminatory if based on similarity rather than performance.

items.answer: Arguments for: Fiedler’s contingency theory shows that task- and relationship-motivated leaders are effective in different situations. items.answer: The theory that leaders form relationships of different quality with each follower, creating in-groups and out-groups.

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “Leaders can be trained to offer high-quality relationships to all followers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Leadership-making training aims to develop partnerships with every follower.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of leader–member exchange (LMX) theory in terms of research support.
items.answer: High-quality LMX has been linked to better performance, satisfaction and lower turnover.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to research support; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: In an engineering team in Lagos, Elena is often given interesting projects and chats with the manager daily, while Diego receives only routine tasks and formal instructions. Explain how this difference may affect Diego’s job satisfaction.
items.answer: Diego receives less support, trust and opportunity, so is likely to be less satisfied and more likely to leave.
items.markingKey: 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A retail chain in Auckland compared customer-satisfaction ratings (out of 100) for 8 stores whose managers had completed training in considerate leadership and 8 stores whose managers had not. Table: Satisfaction score (out of 100) — Trained: 67, 70, 76, 58, 70, 81, 72, 69. Untrained: 64, 63, 65, 63, 54, 68, 60, 51. (a) Calculate the range of scores for each condition. (b) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: (a) Trained: 23; untrained: 17. (b) Team members’ answers about their leader should be anonymous.
items.markingKey: (a) Trained: 81 − 58 = 23; untrained: 68 − 51 = 17. 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: “Leader–member exchange (LMX) theory has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including research support in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): It explains why some employees are more satisfied and committed than others under the same leader. Strength (research support): High-quality LMX has been linked to better performance, satisfaction and lower turnover. Weakness (ethics): It may seem to justify favouritism and unequal treatment of out-group members. Weakness (cause and effect): Most evidence is correlational, so good performance may cause a good relationship rather than the reverse. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Leader behaviour that organises tasks, sets goals and defines roles (Ohio State studies)”?
items.answer: Initiating structure
items.markingKey: Initiating structure: leader behaviour that organises tasks, sets goals and defines roles (Ohio State studies). [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the difference between universalist and behavioural theories of leadership. (b) Describe Blake and Mouton’s managerial grid.
items.answer: (a) Universalist theories focus on who the leader is (traits, charisma) and assume these work everywhere; behavioural theories focus on what the leader does (for example consideration and initiating structure), which can be observed and learned. (b) Leaders are rated 1–9 on concern for production and concern for people; positions include impoverished (1,1), country club (1,9), authority-compliance (9,1), middle of the road (5,5) and team management (9,9), which is seen as ideal.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark universalist; 1 mark behavioural; 1 mark difference made explicit [3] (b) 1 mark two dimensions; 1 mark example styles; 1 mark 9,9 ideal [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “Transformational leaders mainly motivate followers through rewards and punishments.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe Blake and Mouton’s managerial grid.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. That is transactional leadership; transformational leaders inspire with vision and charisma. (b) Leaders are rated 1–9 on concern for production and concern for people; positions include impoverished (1,1), country club (1,9), authority-compliance (9,1), middle of the road (5,5) and team management (9,9), which is seen as ideal.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark two dimensions; 1 mark example styles; 1 mark 9,9 ideal [3]

items.stem: A retail chain in Lisbon compared customer-satisfaction ratings (out of 100) for 6 stores whose managers had completed training in considerate leadership and 6 stores whose managers had not. Table: Satisfaction score (out of 100) — Trained: 66, 79, 70, 67, 61, 71. Untrained: 61, 63, 61, 57, 58, 60. Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice.
items.answer: Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, a new manager at a bank in Cairo, focuses entirely on targets and deadlines and rarely talks to staff about their concerns. Staff turnover has risen. (a) Using the Ohio State dimensions, explain why turnover may have risen. (b) Suggest how Yusuf could become a 9,9 leader.
items.answer: (a) High initiating structure with low consideration leaves staff feeling unvalued, reducing satisfaction and increasing turnover. (b) Keep clear goals while involving staff in decisions, listening to concerns and showing appreciation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark low consideration; 1 mark effect [2] (b) 1 mark people; 1 mark production [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Toronto is interested in whether team members of high-quality LMX relationships are more satisfied than those in low-quality relationships. Design a correlation to test this. Your plan must include: how each co-variable will be measured, how the data will be presented and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a correlation. Measure both co-variables for each participant (for example with a rating scale) and plot a scatter graph; look for direction and strength of the relationship. Variables: co-variable 1: LMX score; co-variable 2: job satisfaction score. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Toronto, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “In Fiedler’s model, how much control the leader has, based on leader–member relations, task structure and position power”?
items.answer: Situational favourableness
items.markingKey: Situational favourableness: in Fiedler’s model, how much control the leader has, based on leader–member relations, task structure and position power. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how path-goal theory predicts the best leadership behaviour. (b) Explain how Fiedler measured leadership style.
items.answer: (a) The leader’s job is to help followers reach goals; directive behaviour suits ambiguous tasks and inexperienced staff, supportive behaviour suits stressful or boring tasks, participative suits capable staff who want involvement, and achievement-oriented suits complex tasks. (b) Leaders rated their least preferred co-worker on 18 bipolar adjective scales (such as unfriendly–friendly) from 1 to 8; a high total shows the leader can still see the co-worker positively (relationship-motivated), a low total shows task motivation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark role of leader; 2 marks matching examples [3] (b) 1 mark LPC rating; 1 mark scoring; 1 mark interpretation [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how Fiedler measured leadership style. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “A high LPC score shows that a leader is task-motivated.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Leaders rated their least preferred co-worker on 18 bipolar adjective scales (such as unfriendly–friendly) from 1 to 8; a high total shows the leader can still see the co-worker positively (relationship-motivated), a low total shows task motivation. (b) Not correct. A high score indicates a relationship-motivated leader.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark LPC rating; 1 mark scoring; 1 mark interpretation [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: A retail chain in Jakarta compared customer-satisfaction ratings (out of 100) for 7 stores whose managers had completed training in considerate leadership and 7 stores whose managers had not. Table: Satisfaction score (out of 100) — Trained: 71, 79, 77, 80, 58, 80, 62. Untrained: 61, 61, 66, 58, 67, 69, 63. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The trained condition had a higher mean (72.4) than the untrained condition (63.6), suggesting that training leaders in consideration increases satisfaction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Ana has just become supervisor of a new team of inexperienced call-centre staff in Auckland. The procedures are unclear and staff are anxious. Explain how Ana’s behaviour should change as staff gain experience.
items.answer: Move towards participative or achievement-oriented behaviour, since experienced staff need less direction and want involvement or challenge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark change; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Amara, a manager in Dubai, completed Fiedler’s LPC scale. The 18 item ratings (1–8) were: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 5, 7, 1, 5, 6, 8, 2, 5, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2. Fiedler classified totals of 73 or more as high LPC and 54 or less as low LPC. Amara’s team has good leader–member relations, an unstructured task and weak position power. (a) Calculate the total LPC score. (b) Identify Amara’s leadership style.
items.answer: (a) 66 (b) In the middle range (neither clearly high nor clearly low LPC)
items.markingKey: (a) Sum of the 18 ratings = 66. 1 mark correct total [1] (b) 66 → in the middle range (neither clearly high nor clearly low LPC) [1]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that effective leadership depends more on the situation than on the leader’s traits?
items.answer: Arguments for: Fiedler’s contingency theory shows that task- and relationship-motivated leaders are effective in different situations. Path-goal theory says leaders should change style to suit followers and tasks. Arguments against: Universalist theories such as charismatic and transformational leadership find some traits linked to success in many situations. Situations are hard to measure, and leaders may be unable to change style easily. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Grace wants to find out which leadership behaviours supervisors in a factory use most often. Design an interview to investigate this. Your plan must include: the type of interview, how the data will be analysed, ethical issues and one example question.
items.answer: Method: an interview. A structured or semi-structured interview with set questions asked in the same order; record and transcribe answers; train interviewers. Variables: behaviour category 1: initiating structure; behaviour category 2: consideration. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Mexico City, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘in-group’?
items.answer: In LMX theory, followers with high-quality relationships with the leader, based on trust and mutual support.
items.markingKey: In-group: in LMX theory, followers with high-quality relationships with the leader, based on trust and mutual support. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: In an engineering team in Hanoi, Tariq is often given interesting projects and chats with the manager daily, while Samuel receives only routine tasks and formal instructions.
